basis.ref: Dividend return and capital gains · Folie 18

prompt: (a) What was the total (realized) return of Bel Air between 31/12/2021 and 31/12/2022, and what was the capital gain rate? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Total return = (P₁ + Div₁)/P₀ − 1 = (51.20 + 1.60)/48.00 − 1 = 10.00%.
Capital gain rate = P₁/P₀ − 1 = 51.20/48.00 − 1 = 6.67%.
The difference, 1.60/48.00 = 3.33%, is the dividend yield.

steps.title: Read the data for 2022
steps.why: The return over one year compares what you have at the end (price plus dividend received) with what you paid at the start.

steps.title: Total return
steps.why: Total return = (end price + dividend) / start price − 1. It counts everything the shareholder receives.

steps.title: Capital gain rate
steps.why: The capital gain rate only looks at the price change and ignores the dividend.

steps.title: Check: the gap is the dividend yield
steps.result: Total return = capital gain rate + dividend yield

pitfalls: Forgetting the dividend in the total return.
Dividing by the end price P₁ instead of the start price P₀.

prompt: (b) Assuming that dividends are immediately reinvested in Bel Air stock, what is the overall return from 31/12/2021 to 31/12/2025? What is the annualized return (geometric average)? Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: Idea: chain the yearly returns
steps.why: If dividends are reinvested, the money grows each year by (1 + total return of that year). Over several years you multiply these growth factors.
lines: Yearly total return: R_t = (P_t + Div_t) / P_{t−1} − 1

steps.title: Overall return 2021–2025
steps.why: Multiply the four growth factors, then subtract 1.

steps.title: Geometric average per year
steps.why: The geometric average is the constant yearly return that gives the same overall result after 4 years: take the 4th root of the growth factor.

pitfalls: Adding the yearly returns instead of multiplying the growth factors (1 + R).
Dividing the overall return by 4 (36.59%/4 = 9.15%) instead of taking the 4th root.

prompt: (c) What is the arithmetic average of the four yearly total returns? Why is it higher than the geometric average? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Arithmetic average = (10.00% + -9.18% + 22.43% + 11.68%)/4 = 8.73%.
It is higher than the geometric average (8.11%) because returns vary from year to year (geometric ≈ arithmetic − ½ × variance). The geometric mean is the realized compound return; the arithmetic mean is the estimate for one future year.

steps.title: The four yearly total returns
steps.why: From part (b): each return = (price + dividend) / previous price − 1.

steps.title: Arithmetic average
steps.why: Simply add the returns and divide by the number of years.

steps.title: Why it is higher than the geometric average (8.11%)
steps.why: Returns that go up and down hurt compounding: after −9.18% you need more than +9.18% to get back. The arithmetic mean ignores this, the geometric mean includes it.
lines: Rule of thumb: geometric ≈ arithmetic − ½ × variance
The more volatile the returns, the bigger the gap.
steps.result: Use the geometric mean for past (realized) performance, the arithmetic mean as an estimate for one future year.

pitfalls: Thinking the two averages should be equal – they are only equal if the return is the same every year.

prompt: You bought 200 shares of a company at EUR 120.00 at the start of the year. During the year the company carries out a 2:1 stock split (each old share becomes two new shares). At year-end it pays a dividend of EUR 0.80 per new share and the share trades at EUR 63.50. What is your return over the year? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Compare the whole position, never the share price across a split.
Start: 200 × 120.00 = 24,000.
End: 400 shares × 63.50 = 25,400 plus dividends 400 × 0.80 = 320.
R = (25,400 + 320 − 24,000)/24,000 = 7.17%.

steps.title: Why the share price alone is misleading
steps.why: After a 2:1 split each old share becomes two new shares, so the price roughly halves. Comparing EUR 120 with EUR 63.50 would suggest a big loss that never happened. Compare the value of your whole position instead.

steps.title: Number of shares after the split
Return
lines: R = (End value − Start value) / Start value

pitfalls: Comparing the price before and after the split: 63.50/120 − 1 = −47% is wrong.
Paying the dividend on 200 shares instead of the 400 new shares.

basis.ref: Quiz: reverse split and dividend · Folie 41

prompt: A stock is worth USD 2.00 at the beginning of the year. During the year the company pays a dividend of USD 0.05 per share and then carries out a 1:5 reverse split (5 old shares become 1 new share). At year-end one new share is worth USD 11.50. What is the return on the investment? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Work per old share (the one bought for USD 2.00).
After the 1:5 reverse split one old share is 1/5 of a new share: 11.50/5 = 2.30.
Add the dividend on the old share: 0.05.
R = (2.30 + 0.05 − 2.00)/2.00 = 17.50%.

steps.title: Work with one old share
steps.why: You paid USD 2.00 for one old share. Follow what happens to exactly this share.

steps.title: Dividend
steps.why: The dividend is paid before the reverse split, so it is paid per old share.

steps.title: Effect of the 1:5 reverse split
steps.why: 5 old shares become 1 new share, so one old share equals 1/5 of a new share.
lines: Value of one old share at year-end = 11.50 / 5

steps.title: Return
lines: R = (End value + Dividend − Start value) / Start value

pitfalls: Comparing 11.50 with 2.00 directly (that would be +475%) – the share count changed.

basis.ref: Quiz: value halved in six months · Folie 41

prompt:
(a) A stock gains 12% in three months. What is the annualized return?
(b) Another stock loses 30% of its value in eight months. What is its annualized return? (No dividends, no splits.) Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: The annualizing rule
steps.why: A return earned over part of a year is turned into a yearly return by compounding: raise the growth factor (1 + R) to the power "12 / number of months" – as if the same return were earned again and again until the year is full.

pitfalls: Multiplying instead of compounding: 12% × 4 = 48% ignores interest on interest.
Using 8/12 as the exponent instead of 12/8.

prompt: Two years ago you bought a share of Return Ltd. In the first year the stock returned +80%, in the second year −51%. Compute the arithmetic average, the geometric average and the total return over the two years. Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Arithmetic: (80% − 51%)/2 = 14.50%.
Total: (1.80)(0.49) − 1 = -11.80%.
Geometric: √(1.80 × 0.49) − 1 = -6.09%.
The arithmetic mean is positive although you lost money – for realized performance use the geometric mean.

steps.title: Growth factors of the two years
Arithmetic average
steps.why: Add the returns and divide by 2.

steps.title: Total return over two years
steps.why: Multiply the growth factors and subtract 1.

steps.title: Geometric average
steps.why: The constant yearly return that gives the same total: take the square root (two years).

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.why: The arithmetic average says +14.5% per year, but you actually lost 11.8%. For past performance only the geometric average is meaningful.

pitfalls: Reporting the arithmetic average as your realized return.

prompt: A stock had the following yearly returns: 8%, −6%, 15%, 3%, 10%. (a) Compute the average return and the volatility (historical data). (b) A second stock has a monthly volatility of 4%. What is its annualized volatility? Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: (a) Average return
steps.why: Add the five returns and divide by 5.

steps.title: (a) Deviations from the mean
steps.why: For each year: return − mean. Work in percentage points to keep numbers simple.

steps.title: (a) Variance and volatility
steps.why: With historical data you divide by T − 1 = 4 (not by T = 5). Volatility is the square root of the variance.

steps.title: (b) Annualize a monthly volatility
steps.why: Variances add up over independent months, so the variance grows with 12 and the volatility with √12.

pitfalls: Dividing by 5 instead of 4 for historical data (gives 7.13%).
Multiplying the monthly volatility by 12 instead of √12.

basis.ref: Critical thinking: return on a bond · Folie 43

prompt: A bond with a face value of EUR 100 trades at EUR 98.50 at the beginning of the year. It pays an annual coupon of 5% of face value at year-end, when it trades at EUR 96.00. What is the return on the bond over the year? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Same logic as a stock: price change plus cash received.
R = (96.00 + 5.00 − 98.50)/98.50 = 2.50/98.50 = 2.54%.
The coupon rate (5%) is not the return.

steps.title: Treat the bond like a stock
steps.why: Return = (price change + cash received) / price paid. For a bond the cash received is the coupon.

pitfalls: Taking the coupon rate (5%) as the return – the price fell, which reduces the return.
Computing the coupon on the price (5% × 98.50) instead of on the face value.

prompt: Explain when you use the arithmetic average and when the geometric average of past returns. Illustrate with a stock that first falls by 50% and then rises by 100%.
modelAnswer: The geometric average (compound annual return, CAGR) measures what an investment actually earned per year in the past: the constant yearly return that turns the initial into the final wealth. The arithmetic average is the best estimate of the expected return of one future period and is used as E(R). They are equal only if all returns are identical; otherwise arithmetic > geometric (≈ arithmetic − ½ variance). Example: −50% then +100% → arithmetic (−50 + 100)/2 = +25%, but 100 → 50 → 100, so the geometric average is 0%: you earned nothing.
keyPoints: Geometric = realized compound return per year (CAGR)
Arithmetic = estimate of next period's expected return
Arithmetic ≥ geometric, equal only for constant returns
